asked_by: Akien, mid-build: '/intent task observer (Claude Code skill) to help us optimize? can we learn anything from it?'
the_answer: SUPERSEDED IN PART 2026-07-27 — see `rebelytics_task_observer` below. The claim 'there is no task observer in Claude Code' stands for the SHIPPED product (no such skill, plugin, hook or SDK feature). It was wrong as an answer to the question Akien was actually asking: a third party had already BUILT one as a skill, and he had the link. ORIGINAL: THERE IS NO 'TASK OBSERVER' IN CLAUDE CODE. Not a skill, not a plugin, not a hook, not an SDK feature — researched against the published docs 2026-07-26. So the question is not 'what can we learn from it' but 'what would we build, and out of what'.

what_actually_exists.hooks_that_can_gate: The interesting half. ~31 hook events, and several can REFUSE, not merely watch: PreToolUse (allow/deny/ask/defer, and can rewrite the tool's input), PostToolUse (can replace the tool's output before the model sees it), PostToolBatch (can block the next model call), TaskCreated / TaskCompleted (exit code 2 prevents the create or the completion). These close a feedback loop inside the running session.
what_actually_exists.read_only_surfaces: PostToolUseFailure, SubagentStart / SubagentStop, TeammateIdle — diagnostic only, after the fact.
what_actually_exists.telemetry: OpenTelemetry export (spans, per-step token counts, tool names, subagent chain) behind CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY. After-the-fact by construction: it exports on an interval, so it cannot gate anything.
what_actually_exists.task_tools: TaskCreate/Update/Get/List — readable mid-turn, so the agent can adjust against its own task state.
what_actually_exists.one_agent_watching_another_live: UNVERIFIED / probably absent. Teammates can message, and a lead can read a teammate's transcript after the fact, but no documented real-time tap on another agent's tool calls was found.

why_this_is_worth_a_node_later: THE GATING HOOKS ARE THE SAME SHAPE CAIRN ALREADY USES. A hook that returns exit code 2 and stops the call is not a supervisor watching and complaining — it is a gate the operation must pass through, which is exactly Cairn's answer to 'who enforces this' (no enforcer; gated ownership — the db_domain pattern, the emit-chokepoint, the projector's single write door). So the host offers physics-shaped primitives, not policy-shaped ones, and a Cairn discipline that today lives as prose in a skill's steps could become a hook that REFUSES. That converts an IOU into enforcement (Law 4) for the class of rules whose subject is CC's own tool use.
candidates_if_it_becomes_current: The rules in CLAUDE.md's 'Rules awaiting physics' whose subject is a TOOL CALL rather than a file's content — e.g. 'durable relational state goes through db_domain' is an import-scan today (tester), but a PreToolUse hook could refuse a write that bypasses the door at the moment it is attempted.

The 'verified on disk before done' correction (memory: verified-on-disk-before-done): a hook on the claim rather than on my habit. TaskCompleted can REFUSE a completion — which is where 'done' could be forced to carry an observation mark instead of being a word I chose.

Rendering a workflow string through transitions.render() rather than by hand — the /sorted IOU in troubles/workflow-cursor-unreadable-by-the-chokepoint.json. A hook that refuses a ticket write whose `state` does not parse would close it as physics.

The measured cost of CC's own work, for the cocoon design (memory: cocoon-settle-stages-around-cc): OTEL gives per-step token counts, which is the instrument that would say whether moving a stage upstream actually pays. Today that claim would be unmeasured.
the_honest_caveat: All of the above is a READ of published capability, not a measurement. Nothing here has been run. Per Law 3 it is a hypothesis about what the host would allow, and the flag names verify-at-build: hook event names and the exit-code-2 semantics must be confirmed against the installed version before anything is built on them, because this is CC reporting on CC's own toolchain — the least independent witness available. This machine's ~/.claude/settings.json currently configures Stop and StopFailure hooks only.

rebelytics_task_observer.what_it_is: A meta-skill that watches a working session, logs corrections/gaps/blind-spots as numbered markdown observations, and produces RECOMMENDATIONS a human applies in a batched review. Author reports ~900 improvements across 50 skills in six months. Pure prose mechanism — no hooks, no gates, no code; the discipline is a list of STEPS the model is told to follow.
rebelytics_task_observer.steal_1_the_principle_field: THE ONE CHEAP, REAL TAKE. Their observation record is {Status, Date, Session context, Skill, Type, Phase/Area, Issue, Suggested improvement, PRINCIPLE — 'the generalisable takeaway'}. Cairn's mark (cairn/base/needs.py, REQUIRED_MARK_FIELDS) is {need, status, when, how_measured} — it records the INSTANCE and nothing above it. Their `Principle` is Law 1's compile step given a FIELD, which is the force-the-why-structurally move (put the generalisation in the schema so it cannot be silently skipped) applied to a place Cairn had not applied it. Cost: one required field + gate + teeth in needs.py, which is PROVED, so it carries a proof cascade — CC's read is that it is worth it, but it is a change to a sealed component and therefore Akien's call.
rebelytics_task_observer.the_gap_that_runs_the_other_way: THEY LOG OPINIONS, WE LOG MEASUREMENTS. Their `Issue` field is 'what happened' — narrative, unmeasured. Cairn's how_measured has a character floor and a gate that refuses a mark without it. This is why '900 improvements' cannot be read as 900 improvements: it counts EDITS, not benefit, and the instrument that would tell the difference does not exist in their design (Law 3). Do not import their record wholesale — import the one field they have that we lack.
rebelytics_task_observer.steal_2_a_shrink_mechanism_cairn_lacks: Their 'simplification signals': sections never relevant across sessions; shortcuts users consistently take; UNVALIDATED SINGLE-OBSERVATION RULES; and agent-failure patterns to 'convert to structural checks or remove'. That last clause is Law 4 arrived at independently. The genuinely useful one is the REMOVAL trigger: CLAUDE.md's 'Rules awaiting physics' promises to shrink monotonically, but its ONLY shrink door is 'the tester enforces it'. There is no door for 'this rule has never fired — delete it'. That is a real hole and they name it. (Note the live tension: their 'unvalidated single-observation rule' is suspect, while Cairn's force-the-why-structurally says catch it at n=1. Both can be right — n=1 is the right moment to WRITE a rule and the wrong evidence to KEEP one. Unresolved, and cheap to leave unresolved.)
rebelytics_task_observer.what_their_discipline_proves_about_our_p: Their SKILL.md spends its longest section on 'pre-write numbering' and 'mutation safety': find the highest existing number, assert no collision, back up the log, re-read the live file immediately before write-back, mutate ONE bounded entry at a time, verify header counts, re-grep post-write to confirm your entries survived. Every line of that is the price of hand-editing a shared record. Cairn pays NONE of it: the projector's append door is the single write door, entries are append-only with a monotonic seq, and `state` is compiled and never hand-edited. An independent builder, working the same problem, wrote out in prose steps exactly the discipline our physics removes — which is the strongest outside evidence yet for Law 4 and the charter-state-history split. CONVERGENT, though: their 're-grep post-write to confirm your entries survived' is memory verified-on-disk-before-done reached from the other direction, and they wrote it into a STEP rather than trusting the agent to remember — which is the same correction CC recorded against itself.
rebelytics_task_observer.reject_the_clock: Their trigger is 'after every 3rd TodoWrite completion' and their review cadence is a weekly / Mon-Wed-Fri session. Both are polls — a counter poll and a clock poll — and they are exactly what memory reaching-for-daemons-is-drift names as where pollers sneak back in. Cairn's version fires on the event that already exists (the correction happens; the gate refuses at the moment of the attempt). Steal the sentence that justifies their poll — 'the write itself enforces the check; remembered mental notes don't survive cognitive load' — and reject the poll: that sentence is an argument for physics, and they settled for a counter.
rebelytics_task_observer.their_gate_is_a_human: 'The observer doesn't modify your skills directly. It produces recommendations that you review.' The SHAPE is right and independently confirms gated ownership (Law 6, no enforcer). The OPERATOR is wrong for us: their gate is a person on a weekly cadence, and Cairn's founding intention is to get Akien out of running the system. Same seam, different gatekeeper.
rebelytics_task_observer.their_own_honest_boundary: Quoted from the README: the log-and-review cycle 'pay[s] off most as your skill library and usage grow... If you run a small setup with a handful of skills, your AI system's built-in memory features may cover much of the same ground with less overhead.' Cairn today is that small setup — a handful of skills and ~20 memories. So the LOG-AND-BATCH half is overhead we should not adopt; the SCHEMA half (one field) is free. Their caveat is doing the work our own build-minimal-grow-against-need would do.
rebelytics_task_observer.still_unmeasured: Nothing here was run. This is a READ of someone else's prose, and the headline number (900 improvements) is self-reported and uninstrumented. Law 3 — hypothesis, labelled.
